newsitem.title: UK: Sterling strength a godsend for BOE and Treasury.
newsitem.headline: Sterling strength a godsend for BOE and Treasury.

text.p: Sterling's current strength is having the same effect as the monetary tightening urged by the Bank of England and is good news for the government, fighting to avert an interest rate rise ahead of a looming general election.
But a climbing pound could hit exports as Britain's competitive advantage erodes, analysts said on Thursday.

"In other centres if the currency looks like getting too strong you get central bank comments or government comments worried that it's going to affect the export performance," said Pat Magill, head of the corporate desk at Daiwa Europe.
"As yet there've been no real comments or signs that the government or the Bank of England are going to resist it."

And why should they resist? While Bank of England governor Eddie George urges tightening to fend off the inflationary risks of an accelerating economy, finance minister Kenneth Clarke is desperate to hold rates steady or even cut them.

"For Mr Clarke it's nicely timed, because we've had a pretty long run of strong economic activity now which has bolstered Mr George in his demands for higher interest rates," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets in London.
"This (sterling strength) counts in Kenneth Clarke's favour if he wants to keep rates unchanged."

Sterling has risen 3.9 percent against the mark and 2.1 percent on a trade-weighted basis in just over a month as robust British monetary and economic activity indicators have thrown cold water on the prospects of another base rate cut ahead of the elections, which must be held by next May.
Analysts said it is axiomatic here that a four percent sterling appreciation is equivalent to a one percentage-point rise in base rates, which currently stand at 5.75 percent.

"You're seeing an effective monetary policy tightening and from that point of view the Bank of England are probably not overly concerned, because they've been arguing monetary policy should be tightenened. This is a different way of getting it," said UK economist Ciaran Barr at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Market watchers offer a variety of reasons for sterling's bull run. Economic activity is improving but inflation remains subdued, while better than expected second-quarter UK current account data released last month soothed fears that brisk growth will suck in imports and balloon the current account deficit.

Meantime the market is growing happier with the idea that the next election will sweep the opposition Labour party to power after 17 years of Conservative government, and thinking the unthinkable, that a Labour government could even boost the pound.

But many analysts say all these domestic factors are secondary to the fact that yield-hungry investors are swarming out of currencies like yen and marks for those such as Italian lire, Swedish crowns and sterling.
"Basically it's just a flow of money effect -- sterling's seen as being one of the high yielder currencies and they've been doing very well," said Barr at Deutsche.
Sterling hit 2.4018 marks in European trading on Thursday, its best level in 20 months. It has also scored three and a half year highs against a generally depressed yen in recent days.
But though the Treasury and the Bank of England might be happy to sit back now and watch sterling going from strength to strength, some anticipate protests if the rally rolls too far.
"When sterling was sold off (the authorities) were loving it because it was giving us a competitive advantage. That competitive advantage is being eroded," said Daiwa's Magill.

Others note, however, that British exports have performed well in recent months despite sterling's upward mobility. The Confederation of British Industry said on Thursday that UK exporters had not yet felt the pinch of currency strength.

"Exports have been holding up remarkably robustly so far this year in the face of pretty weak overseas markets and export prices have been falling, which suggests UK firms are keen to maintain their competitiveness," said HSBC's Loynes.
